analysis.one_liner: Makes large gig companies pay Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes on their independent contractors.
analysis.headline: The bill sits in the House Ways and Means Committee with 8 Democratic sponsors and no committee action as Congress nears its January 3, 2027 end.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, companies that hire people as independent contractors don't pay the payroll taxes that fund Social Security and Medicare — the workers do, out of their own pay, and many gig workers end up with little or no Social Security credit for those earnings. This bill would flip that for the biggest companies: any business with over $100 million in revenue and at least 10,000 contractors would have to treat those payments like wages, pay the employer's share, and pay double the usual employer rate — effectively covering the tax burden for the worker. The workers would also get Social Security credit for their gig earnings. It was introduced June 2, 2026 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which has taken no action on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent contractors — drivers, delivery workers, freelancers — who work for very large companies would gain: the company would shoulder the payroll tax they currently pay themselves, and their gig earnings would count toward their future Social Security benefits.

how_it_helps.text: Businesses with $100 million or more in gross receipts and at least 10,000 independent contractors must treat those contractor payments as wages for income tax withholding and employment tax purposes.

The employer tax rate under section 3111 would be multiplied by 2, meaning the large company pays the full payroll tax on contractor earnings rather than the worker paying both halves as self-employment tax.

The bill amends the Social Security Act so amounts treated as wages under the new rule count as earnings for the worker's Social Security benefits, giving gig workers retirement credit they often lack today.
Related companies under common ownership are treated as a single employer, so a company cannot avoid the rule by splitting itself into many small entities.

analysis.who_pays: Very large companies that rely on independent contractor labor — such as big ride-hailing, delivery, and other gig platforms — would pay a payroll tax on contractor pay they do not pay today, roughly doubling their effective payroll tax rate on that work.

drawbacks.text: Doubling the employer-side rate would significantly raise the cost of contractor labor for large platforms, which could cut contractor pay, set minimum work requirements, or shift toward full employment with less schedule flexibility — the very flexibility many gig workers value.
The higher tax cost could be passed on to consumers through higher prices for rides and deliveries.
Requiring wage treatment for income tax withholding changes how contractors receive and file their pay, which some contractors and tax practitioners would need to adjust to.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the benefit is real and concrete: the company pays the tax and their gig earnings count toward Social Security, ending a gap where millions of workers effectively go without retirement credit. The main cost falls on the largest platforms, and some of it could reach workers through lower pay or consumers through higher prices, but the bill applies only to companies over $100 million in revenue with 10,000 or more contractors, leaving smaller businesses and genuinely independent contractors untouched.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which has not scheduled any action, so it awaits whatever happens before Congress ends on January 3, 2027.

narrative.text: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman introduced the bill in the House on June 2, 2026, with seven Democratic cosponsors.
The House referred the bill to the Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
The bill's complete action history shows only those two actions, with no hearing, markup, or floor vote.
The bill's provisions would take effect for payments made after December 31, 2026 if enacted.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no outcome has been reached. Large gig platforms remain better off for the time being: they continue paying no employer payroll tax on contractor earnings while the bill sits without committee action.

for.name: Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the House and recruited seven Democratic cosponsors.

for.name: Reps. Lee of Pennsylvania, McIver, Hayes, Tlaib, Adams, Omar, and Ramirez

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote — in the six months since referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 8 sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican support appears in the record.

industries.industry: Gig economy platforms (ride-hailing, delivery, freelance marketplaces)
industries.note: Large platforms would owe a doubled employer payroll tax on contractor earnings and their contractors would gain Social Security coverage. Under current law these companies avoid the employer share of payroll taxes entirely on this workforce, which is what the bill targets.

industries.industry: Small and mid-sized businesses using contractors
industries.note: The bill's thresholds ($100 million revenue, 10,000 contractors) exempt them from the new withholding and payroll tax obligation, so they face no added cost while their large competitors bear one.

analysis.trajectory: A bill this early with eight sponsors, all from one party, and no committee action has a low chance of becoming law before Congress ends on January 3, 2027. Absent a leadership decision to schedule it, the most likely path is that it dies in committee at the end of this Congress.
